amendments.summary: Haryana has not amended Section 138 (or ss.139 to 147) of the Negotiable Instruments Act - the offence, the presumptions, the notice period, limitation and compounding are uniform central law. What sits here is Haryana's own State Act that bears on a cheque case: the Haryana Police Act, 2007, which constitutes the force that serves the court's process and executes its warrants. Court fees are not a separate Haryana Act - Haryana still levies them under the central Court-Fees Act, 1870 as amended in its application to the State (Haryana Acts 11 and 22 of 1974, 27 of 1976 and 3 of 1990), whose Schedule II Article 1(b) fixes ten rupees on a complaint presented to a criminal court. That is the Rs.10 court-fee ticket the Panchkula filing assistants describe. No official consolidated Haryana text of that Act is published (India Code carries no Haryana entry for it), so it is not converted here; the operative fee tables are under Notifications. The rules of practice, e-filing and video conferencing are under State rules.

items.title: Haryana Police Act, 2007
items.cite: Haryana Act 25 of 2008 · State police law
items.note: The State police law for Haryana - it constitutes the force, the ranks and units, the appointment of the Director General, the police districts and the police stations. A cheque-bounce case is a complaint case with no FIR, no investigation and no arrest at the outset, so the police enter only once the court issues process: the Station House Officer serves the summons and executes a bailable or non-bailable warrant. The Haryana counterpart of the Kerala Police Act, 2011.

key.label: Role and functions of the police
key.note: The general duties of the Haryana Police, closing with the residual duty to enforce any other duty assigned by law. That residual duty is the hook through which a s.138 case reaches the police at all: there is no investigation to do, but the court's summons and warrants have to be served and executed by someone.

key.label: Police stations and the Station House Officer
key.note: Creates the police stations and their outposts by notification and puts a Station House Officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector in charge of each. This is the station that receives and serves the court's process in a cheque case, and the station the Panchkula filing branch records against the file - derived from the bank where the cheque was presented - even though a s.138 case never generates an FIR.

key.label: Appointment of the Director General of Police
key.note: Puts the overall direction and supervision of the police service in a Director General appointed by the State Government. It touches a cheque case only at one remove - it is the command chain above the officer who ends up serving the summons or executing the warrant the magistrate issues.

key.label: Sums paid for the service of processes by police officers
key.note: Directs the sums paid for the service of processes by police officers to the State account. It is the fee side of the same act the court relies on when it sends a s.138 summons or warrant out through the police, and the State law's own acknowledgement that serving court process is police work.

rules.summary: How a s.138 case is actually filed and tried in Haryana. The subordinate criminal courts of Haryana run on the Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, a multi-volume compendium the High Court makes under Articles 225 and 227 of the Constitution. Volume III, Instructions to Criminal Courts, is the Haryana counterpart of Kerala's Criminal Rules of Practice: it governs cognizance on a complaint, the issue of process, the conduct of the trial, the judgment, sentence and appeal. Written on top of it are two newer High Court rule sets that a cheque case now meets first - the Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules and the Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, both of which reach the district judiciary through the High Court's supervisory jurisdiction.

items.title: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts)
items.cite: High Court rules of practice · criminal courts
items.note: The core Haryana instrument for how a criminal court runs a case. Volume III is the High Court's standing instructions to the subordinate criminal courts of Punjab, Haryana and U.T. Chandigarh, and it covers the whole spine of a cheque case: initiation of proceedings and cognizance on a complaint (Chapter 1 Part B), the attendance of the accused and the summons or warrant choice (Part C), the procedure in trials by magistrates (Part D), the record of evidence (Part E), dismissal of cases in default (Part F), the judgment and compounding (Part H), video conferencing (Part BB), summary trials (Chapter 2), bail (Chapter 10), proceedings against absconders (Chapter 15), sentences and fine (Chapter 19), the Probation of Offenders Act (Chapter 21) and appeal and revision (Chapter 25). The High Court publishes Volume III as about a hundred separate chapter and part PDFs; all 31 chapters are stitched here in publication order, and the stored PDF is that stitched copy. The source uses a marginal-note layout - the paragraph heading is printed in a side column - so the side notes have been lifted into the rule headings; a few headings in the older small-capitals chapters come out of the publisher's text layer scrambled, and the rule text itself carries the occasional typographic error of the original. Verify a rule against the official copy at highcourtchd.gov.in before relying on its exact words. The Volume still cites the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 and 1973 by their old section numbers; read those through the 2024 Sanhita mapping.

key.label: Examination of the complainant on taking cognizance
key.note: The first duty of a magistrate taking cognizance of an offence on a complaint is to examine the complainant. This is the moment a cheque complaint becomes a case: the complainant's sworn statement, with the cheque, the bank return memo and the demand notice, is what the magistrate weighs before deciding to issue process.

key.label: Place of inquiry or trial
key.note: Jurisdiction turns on the place where the offence was committed, with the exceptions that follow for offences uncertain in place, committed partly in one area, or continuing. For a cheque case s.142(2) of the NI Act displaces the general rule with its own test - the branch of the bank where the payee maintains the account - so this is where the local practice and the special statute meet.

key.label: Summons or e-summons, and dismissal for unpaid process fee
key.note: As amended in November 2018, a magistrate may issue a summons or an e-summons in his discretion, and must record reasons before issuing a warrant where the law provides for a summons. It also carries the rule that bites hardest on a cheque complainant: where process fees are payable no process issues until they are paid, and on default within a reasonable time the magistrate may dismiss the complaint.

edges.rel: warrant in lieu of summons under

key.label: When the attendance of the accused may be dispensed with
key.note: A criminal trial is conducted in the presence of the accused, but the court has a discretion to dispense with personal attendance and permit an advocate to appear. This is the everyday relief in a cheque case, where the accused is often out of station and the trial is meant to be summary.

key.label: Video conferencing in criminal matters
key.note: Inserted in December 2021 following the Supreme Court's Model Rules: the procedure for video conferencing in criminal matters in the subordinate courts is the Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts in Volume V, Chapter 1, Part H. This single line is the hook by which a cheque case before a Haryana magistrate can take evidence, or the appearance of a party, over a live link.

key.label: Summons case: the complainant's non-attendance
key.note: In a summons case instituted on a complaint, if the complainant fails to attend on a day fixed for hearing the magistrate may acquit the accused. A s.138 case is tried as a summons case, so this is the sharpest procedural risk the complainant carries at every single date.

key.label: Dismissal in default - reasons must be recorded
key.note: Before dismissing a case because the complainant is absent the magistrate must consider whether such an order is legal and whether it is justified, and record his reasons. Part F opens by warning that magistrates are inclined to dismiss in default too hastily. It is the check on the risk in rule 1-D.5, and the ground on which a dismissed cheque complaint is revived in revision.

key.label: Who may hold a summary trial, and how
key.note: Summary trials may be held only by a magistrate of the first class specially empowered, or a Bench so empowered, and Chapter 2 sets out the procedure and its limits. Section 143 of the NI Act directs that a cheque case be tried summarily, so this chapter is the local manual for the trial a s.138 complaint actually gets.

edges.rel: operationalises the summary trial directed by

key.label: Acquittal when the offence is compounded
key.note: Compounding an offence has the effect of an acquittal, and the court must record it that way rather than as a withdrawal or a dismissal. Section 147 of the NI Act makes every offence under the Act compoundable and most cheque cases end in a settlement, so this is how a Haryana magistrate writes up the end of the case.

key.label: Fine to be proportionate to the offender's means
key.note: A fine is the lightest punishment a criminal court can impose, but it must not be excessive with reference to the means of the offender. On a s.138 conviction the fine may run to twice the amount of the cheque, so this is the state-level counterweight a magistrate applies when fixing it, and the reason default imprisonment has its own limits.

items.title: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana
items.cite: High Court rules · e-filing (R&O Vol.V Ch.1 Part J)
items.note: The rules that govern filing a case electronically in Haryana. They were inserted into the Rules and Orders as Volume V, Chapter 1, Part J by Correction Slip No. 190 dated 7 February 2023, and they apply not only to the High Court but to every court and tribunal over which it has supervisory jurisdiction - which is how they reach the district courts where a cheque complaint is filed. They amend and consolidate the earlier e-filing rules and practice directions, and the definition of an Action expressly includes criminal complaints, so a s.138 complaint is inside the regime. Twenty rules plus six appendices of screenshots; the appendices are in the source PDF but are not converted.

key.label: Applicability and commencement
key.note: The rules bind the High Court and every court and tribunal under its supervisory jurisdiction, cover both online e-filing and filing at a designated counter or e-Sewa Kendra, and amend and consolidate the earlier rules and practice directions. This is the clause that carries the e-filing regime down to the Haryana district court where a cheque complaint is filed.

key.label: Definitions - an Action includes a criminal complaint
key.note: An Action expressly includes criminal complaints, so a s.138 complaint is within the e-filing rules and not merely a civil-side facility. The same rule defines the Administrator - for a district court, the officer appointed by the District and Sessions Judge - which is the formal name for the office the Panchkula filing assistants call the computer room and must telephone before an e-filed case can be released into their queue.

key.label: Formatting and the OCR-searchable PDF
key.note: All original typed material must be prepared as the Rules and Orders require, converted into an optical-character-recognition searchable PDF, and non-text documents scanned to a stated standard. This is the bar the cheque, the bank return memo and the legal notice have to clear before the filing branch will take the file.

key.label: Digital signatures
key.note: The PDF must be digitally signed by the party or the advocate, from a recognised provider, with a fallback where the filer holds no digital signature. It is the electronic form of the page-by-page attestation the Panchkula window checks on a physical NACT file.

key.label: Payment of court fees and other charges
key.note: Court fee may be paid electronically through the authorised agency, at a designated counter, or from an authorised court-fee vendor, and the transaction ID must be entered at the time of e-filing. This is where the ten rupee complaint fee actually changes hands when a cheque case is filed online instead of over the counter.

key.label: Retention of originals
key.note: Originals of the scanned documents must be preserved for production or inspection, signed vakalatnamas and attested affidavits for at least two years after final disposal including appeal, and the burden of producing the originals and proving their genuineness falls on the party that filed the scans. Rule 11.3 keeps negotiable instruments permanently but expressly excepts a cheque, so the cheque - the whole case - sits under the general rule and has to be produced when the court calls for it.

key.label: Exemption from e-filing
key.note: The Bench may exempt a pleading or a document from e-filing where it is not feasible, where confidentiality is in issue, where the document cannot be scanned because of its size, shape or condition, or where the portal is unavailable. The escape hatch a complainant needs when the physical cheque or a damaged document will not scan.

edges.rel: exempts filing of the complaint under

key.label: Computation of time
key.note: The date of e-filing is the date the Action is electronically received in the Registry within the prescribed time on a working day, reckoned in Indian Standard Time; a filing made after midnight counts as the next day, and one made on a holiday as the next working day. Limitation is the same regime as physical filing. Decisive for the one month window in s.142(1)(b) of the NI Act, which is exactly the point the Panchkula assistants scrutinise before accepting a NACT file.

key.label: Rejection and objections
key.note: An e-filing that does not follow the protocol is rejected; the Registry communicates objections by e-mail or SMS and the case is processed for listing only once they are cleared. The digital form of the defect loop the filing branch runs at the counter, and the reason an advocate is still told verbally to attach a delay-condonation application.

items.title: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana
items.cite: High Court rules · video conferencing (R&O Vol.V Ch.1 Part H)
items.note: The High Court's video conferencing rules, made under Articles 225 and 227 on the Supreme Court's Model Rules and inserted as Volume V, Chapter 1, Part H by Correction Slip No. 188 dated 10 December 2021. Volume III, Chapter 1, Part BB makes them the procedure for criminal matters in the subordinate courts, so they are the rules a Haryana magistrate applies when a cheque case is heard, or evidence taken, over a live link. Nineteen rules in five chapters: general principles, facilities, preparatory arrangements and coordinators, the procedure for appearance and examination, costs and conduct.

key.label: General principles governing video conferencing
key.note: Video conferencing may be used at all stages of judicial proceedings, and proceedings conducted that way are judicial proceedings for every purpose. That equivalence is what lets a cheque case run a hearing, or take a deposition, remotely without losing its character as a trial.

key.label: Preparatory arrangements, and the accessibility duty in rule 5.9
key.note: Who coordinates at each end, which places count as remote points, the thirty-minute readiness check, the bar on prompting the person being examined, and the record sent ahead to the remote coordinator. Rule 5.9 carries the accessibility duty: whenever required the Court shall order the coordinator to provide a translator where the person to be examined is not conversant with the official language of the Court, an expert in sign languages where the person is impaired in speech and/or hearing, and an interpreter or a special educator where the person is differently abled, temporarily or permanently. In a §138 trial that is the moment the duty bites - the deaf accused answering the notice of accusation, the disabled complainant put to cross-examination. The list stops at the special educator: like Kerala rule 5(9), and unlike Gujarat rule 10(4)(d), there is no limb for a person to read documents aloud to a visually challenged participant. The rules cite no statute for the duty.

key.label: Application for appearance, evidence and submission by video conferencing
key.note: How a party or a witness asks to appear, depose or make submissions over a live link, how the court decides after hearing everyone concerned, and how it fixes the date and the costs. For a cheque case this is the route by which an out-of-station complainant, or a bank official, is spared the journey to the trial court.

key.label: Service of summons for a video conferencing hearing
key.note: A summons to a witness who is to be examined by video conferencing must state the date, time and venue of the remote point and direct the witness to attend there in person with proof of identity. It is the summons a s.138 trial court issues to the bank witness who will prove the return memo remotely.

key.label: Examination of persons over the link
key.note: Identity proof before examination, the oath, working-hours scheduling, the court's power to record demeanour and note objections, the audio-visual recording, and the signature of the person examined on the transcript with a printout route where digital signatures are not available at both ends. These are the mechanics by which the complainant or a bank official proves the cheque and the return memo without attending court.

key.label: Exhibiting documents to a witness at a remote point
key.note: How a document is shown to a person being examined at a remote point when it becomes necessary in the course of the examination. In a cheque case the documents are the whole case - the cheque, the return memo, the demand notice - so this rule decides whether a remote deposition can do the work of an in-person one.

key.label: Framing of charge and examination of the accused by video conferencing
key.note: The court may, in its discretion, authorise detention, frame charges and examine the accused over a video link. In a summary cheque trial the equivalent steps are the notice of accusation and the examination of the accused, so this rule is what lets the whole middle of a s.138 trial happen without the accused travelling.

key.label: Costs, including the fee for the interpreter
key.note: Who bears the cost of a remote hearing, and on what the court may take into account when apportioning it. Rule 13.1 counts the fee payable to the translator, interpreter or special educator among the expenses of the facility, so the support rule 5.9 promises is priced to a party rather than funded by the court, with 13.4 leaving it open to waive the costs. Gujarat rule 22(a) and Kerala rule 12(1) price it the same way. On DRISTI's reading that sits awkwardly with the access-to-justice duty in the RPwD Act, which speaks of the State ensuring access rather than a disabled litigant buying it; the rules do not engage with the question.

key.label: Access to legal aid clinics, camps, Lok Adalats and Jail Adalats
key.note: Persons may take part in legal aid clinics, camps, Lok Adalats and Jail Adalats over a live link, in conformity with the Legal Services Authorities Act. A large share of cheque cases are settled in Lok Adalat, so this is the digital route into the settlement track that ends most s.138 matters.

items.title: Implementation of e-filing 3.0 in the District Courts of Punjab, Haryana and U.T. Chandigarh
items.cite: Registrar General, Punjab and Haryana High Court, 12 February 2024
items.note: The circular by which the district judiciary migrated from e-filing 1.0 to the national e-filing 3.0 software, addressed to every District and Sessions Judge in Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh on the directions of the High Court's Computer Committee and approved by the Acting Chief Justice. Its five directions set the changeover calendar: e-filing of fresh cases accepted only till 14 February 2024, physical filing only from 15 to 22 February, four days of migration downtime from 19 to 22 February, e-filing resuming on the 3.0 portal from 23 February, and compulsory e-filing from 15 March 2024. Direction (iii) is the one that bites on a litigant: pending drafts and cases left under objection in the 'Not Accepted' folder were not migrated and their history was erased, expressly causing loss of exemption of limitation and of delay days. It is the system the Panchkula filing branch works in when an advocate e-files a NACT case, and the reason an e-filed case has to be released by the computer room before the branch can edit and submit it.

key.label: e-filing 3.0 circular, direction (ii) - physical filing only, 15 to 22 February 2024
key.note: For eight days the e-filing channel was shut and a fresh complaint could only be presented across the counter. It is the concrete reason a Panchkula cheque complaint instituted in that window exists on paper rather than in the portal, and it fixes the boundary between the two filing regimes.

key.label: e-filing 3.0 circular, direction (iii) - clear drafts and objected filings by 17 February 2024 or lose them
key.note: The direction with real consequences for a complainant. Anything left in the 'Drafts' folder, and any case sitting under objection in the 'Not Accepted' folder, was not migrated: the data was erased and the case history lost, expressly 'leading to loss of exemption of limitation and delay of days also'. For a cheque complaint that turns on the one-month window in section 142(1)(b) and any condonation sought under its proviso, an erased filing history is the difference between a complaint in time and one that has to be re-filed with an application to condone.

items.title: Court Fee Table, Punjab and Haryana High Court
items.cite: High Court of Punjab and Haryana · court fee schedule
items.note: The fee payable on each case type at the High Court, now browsable as structured text: a row for every case type across the civil writ, civil, company, criminal, Letters Patent and common-documents tables, plus the full Table of Rates of ad valorem fees leviable on the institution of suits under the Court-fees Act, 1870. On the criminal side a criminal revision (CRR), a quashing or transfer petition (CRM-M), an appeal against acquittal (CRM-A) and a criminal miscellaneous application (CRM) all cost Rs.2.65 - the price of taking a s.138 conviction up in revision, or asking the High Court to quash the complaint - and no fee at all is charged where the petitioner is in custody. Annexures are charged at Rs.0.65 a page and a power of attorney at Rs.2.65, which is what a bank or NBFC complainant actually pays on the paper of a cheque case. Note 1 records that fees are still received under the un-amended Court Fees Act, 1870 because Schedules I and II of the Court Fees (Punjab Second Amendment) Act, 2009 stand stayed since 27 November 2013 in RSA No.3311 of 2013, so the chart is expressly provisional. The trial court side is governed by the Court-Fees Act, 1870 as amended in its application to Haryana, whose Schedule II Article 1(b) fixes ten rupees on a complaint presented to a criminal court.

key.label: Court Fee Table - Quashing Petition (CRM-M): Rs. 2.65
key.note: What an accused pays to ask the High Court to quash a cheque complaint: two rupees sixty-five paise. The fee is not the obstacle; the threshold is. This is the price of the inherent-powers route that a s.138 accused most often tries before facing trial.

key.label: Court Fee Table - Criminal Revision (CRR): Rs. 2.65, nil if the petitioner is in custody
key.note: The fee on taking a s.138 conviction or sentence up in revision to the High Court, and nil where the petitioner is in custody. Revision is the ordinary route against a magistrate's or sessions court's order in a cheque case that is not appealable, so this row is the actual out-of-pocket cost of that remedy.

key.label: Court Fee Table - Criminal Appeal, Single Bench (CRA-S): Rs. 2.65 on bail, nil in custody
key.note: The fee a convicted drawer pays to appeal a s.138 conviction where the appeal lies to the High Court, with no fee at all if the appellant is in custody. It is the second half of the picture the trial-court fee gives: cheap to appeal, and free if the sentence has already put the appellant inside.

key.label: Court Fee Table - Criminal Appeal against Acquittal (CRM-A): Rs. 2.65
key.note: The complainant's side of the ledger. When a cheque complaint ends in acquittal, the payee's remedy is an appeal against acquittal to the High Court with special leave, and this row prices it at two rupees sixty-five paise. Cost is not what deters a complainant from appealing; leave is.

key.label: Court Fee Table - Criminal Misc. Application (CRM): Rs. 2.65
key.note: The catch-all interlocutory application in the High Court's criminal side - exemption from personal appearance, stay of proceedings, condonation, placing documents on record. In a cheque matter a party usually files several of these for every substantive petition, and each carries this fee.

key.label: Court Fee Table - no court fee where the appellant, applicant or petitioner is in custody
key.note: The one distributive rule in the criminal table: custody waives the fee outright. A drawer already serving the sentence imposed for dishonour of a cheque pays nothing to move the High Court. It removes the fee as a barrier at exactly the point where a person is least able to pay it.

key.label: Court Fee Table - Annexures: Rs. 0.65 per page
key.note: The per-page charge that actually adds up in a cheque matter. The paper a s.138 case travels on - the cheque, the return memo, the demand notice, the postal receipts, the account statement, the complaint and the trial court's order - is all annexure, and each page is charged separately from the fee on the petition itself.

key.label: Court Fee Table - Power of Attorney: Rs. 2.65
key.note: Cheque complaints are overwhelmingly filed by banks, non-banking financial companies and companies acting through an authorised representative, so the power of attorney is a standing annexure in this case type and carries its own fee.

key.label: Court Fee Table - Note 1: fee charged under the un-amended Court Fees Act, 1870, the 2009 Punjab amendment being stayed
key.note: Why the figures in this table are in rupees and paise rather than modern amounts. Fees are received by the DRR Section under the Court Fees Act, 1870 as un-amended, because Schedules I and II of the Court Fees (Punjab Second Amendment) Act, 2009 were stayed by order dated 27 November 2013 in RSA No. 3311 of 2013 - and the whole chart is expressly subject to the final decision in that case. Anyone relying on these amounts should know the schedule is provisional.

vocabulary.summary: The words the Haryana layer adds on top of the shared national vocabulary. Two sources feed it: a June 2026 field interview with the filing assistants of the Panchkula district courts, which gives the filing-branch roles, the e-Courts CIS mechanics and the local workarounds a s.138 ('NACT') filing runs on; and the Punjab and Haryana High Court's own instruments - Volume III of the Rules and Orders, the Electronic Filing Rules and the Rules for Video Conferencing - which give the court-process, establishment, e-filing and remote-hearing words a cheque case meets after it is filed.

terms.gloss: The filing-branch clerk who receives a s.138 (NACT) file at the lower-court filing window, checks it for completeness and attestation, enters it in the e-Courts CIS, assigns the NACT filing number and CNR number, records it in the register and hands it to the peon for same-day dispatch to the trial court. A formal court-staff role; some of the practices around it (an emailed PDF copy, parking the police station under 'offence remarks') are self-started and outside any rule.
terms.source: Punjab & Haryana lower-court filing branch; described by the filing assistants, Panchkula (PUCAR field interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The record-keeper and process clerk of a criminal court. He receives the file from the filing branch once it has a filing number, registers the case in CIS after the objections are removed and the main case number issues, enters the parties and addresses, and from then on owns the court's process: generating and publishing summons and warrants, entering bail bonds and sureties, attaching the service reports the process servers bring back, keeping the registers, binding and consigning the decided file, and building the monthly returns the High Court asks for. Volume III recognises the office directly - talbana and stamped postal envelopes filed by litigants are received by the ahlmad or the moharrir against a receipt and never by any other member of the ministerial establishment, and the registers of a magistrate's court are maintained by the ahlmad attached to it. He is not the reader: Volume III names the reader of the court separately, and at Panchkula the reader raises the objections and keeps the dates while the ahlmad registers, generates process and keeps the record.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.4 and rule 11-A.14; described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The office that holds the CIS permission to release ('consume' or approve) an e-filed case into the filing branch's queue. The filing assistants have no direct access, so they telephone the computer room each time an e-filing arrives - often ten to fifteen times a day - before they can edit and submit it. 'Computer room' is the local name, and two different offices sit behind it. The E-Filing Rules create the Administrator, who for a district court is the officer appointed by the District and Sessions Judge, for everything connected with e-filing. Separately, every court location has its own technical establishment - a System Officer and a System Assistant - who run the CIS server and its permissions and who are very probably the people the branch actually rings. Which of the two holds the release permission has not been established. An access-control chokepoint rather than a rule.
terms.source: Local CIS access arrangement, Panchkula district courts (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The Case Information System - the national e-Courts case-management software the court works in from filing to judgment. The filing assistant logs in, opens the filing counter, chooses Criminal and then the NACT case type, and enters the party, court-fee and Act details; the system then issues the case numbers. A known pain point is that civil and criminal columns appear together, inviting mis-clicks. At the far end of the case the judgment writer logs in to lift the judgment template, the CNR number and the registration and institution dates, then uploads and e-signs the judgment and runs the reporting that shows which of his orders are still pending upload; orders can be uploaded in a batch but each has to be selected one at a time, and there is no bulk download. It belongs to NIC, not to the High Court: the versions reported were 1.0 from 2011, 2.0 from 2014, 3.0 from 2017 and 4.0 from 2025, and each district court location runs its own instance on its own server, syncing case data to the NJDG in real time while orders and judgments are pushed each evening. A High Court cannot change the core - a suggestion goes to NIC and moves only if the Supreme Court eCommittee approves - so anything a court needs for itself is built beside CIS as a read-only peripheral application.
terms.source: e-Courts Project, Supreme Court e-Committee - Case Information System (CIS)

terms.gloss: The Case Number Record - a nationally unique 16-character identifier the e-Courts system assigns to every case, used to track and search it across courts. In Panchkula the CNR begins 'HRPK' (Haryana, Panchkula). The filing assistant writes it on the file cover alongside the NACT number.
terms.source: e-Courts Project - CNR (Case Number Record), the nationally unique case identifier

terms.gloss: The filing number the CIS generates for a Negotiable Instruments Act case. 'NACT' is the e-Courts case-type code for a s.138 cheque-bounce complaint; selecting it under Criminal and submitting the party and Act details produces the NACT number, which is written on the file cover.
terms.source: e-Courts CIS case-type code for Negotiable Instruments Act s.138 complaints (NACT)

terms.gloss: The list of the parties to the case - the complainant and each respondent with their address and phone number - filed as part of the complaint set. It is a mandatory, scrutinised document; the filing assistant checks that the address and phone fields are present because they are needed for service and registration.
terms.source: Standard pleading in the filed set; scrutinised at the filing window (Panchkula, PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: A free-text field in the CIS filing form that the assistants use to park the jurisdictional police station, because the filing counter has no dedicated column for it. The police station is derived from the bank where the cheque was presented and is used to distribute NACT cases among the clerks - not for any investigation, since a s.138 case has no FIR.
terms.source: Local CIS data-entry practice, Panchkula filing branch (PUCAR interview, June 2026) - a workaround for a missing field

terms.gloss: The lower-court counter where advocates submit physical NACT files and the filing assistant receives, scrutinises and enters them. In Panchkula the window is open until 12:00 PM and files are processed the same day; it handles 40 to 50 files of all categories a day, of which up to about 10 are NACT. It is the modern form of the Volume III petition box, and it sits beside the designated counters and e-Service Centres at which the same complaint may be filed electronically. Court and office timings across the subordinate courts of Haryana are fixed by rule: court from 10:00 to 16:30, office from 09:30 to 17:00.
terms.source: Panchkula district courts filing branch (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The Punjab and Haryana High Court's standing instructions to the subordinate criminal courts of Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh - the Haryana counterpart of Kerala's Criminal Rules of Practice. Volume III governs the whole spine of a cheque case: cognizance on a complaint, the issue of process, the conduct of the trial, the record of evidence, dismissal in default, the judgment, the sentence and the appeal. It is made under the High Court's powers of superintendence in Articles 225 and 227 of the Constitution, and it opens at Chapter 1 Part A with the uniform court and office timings for every subordinate court in the two States. It still cites the old Codes of 1898 and 1973 by their former section numbers, so it has to be read through the 2024 Sanhita mapping.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.1

terms.gloss: The first duty of a magistrate taking cognizance on a complaint: to examine the complainant, and any witnesses present, on oath and to record the substance of that examination in writing, signed by the complainant, the witnesses and the magistrate. Volume III insists it is not a formality - it is what tells the magistrate whether to put the machinery of the criminal court in motion or to dismiss the complaint for want of sufficient ground. In a cheque case this is the moment the complaint becomes a case, and in practice the s.145 affidavit does much of the work.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-B.4

terms.gloss: An electronic summons. Since the November 2018 amendment to Volume III a magistrate may, in his discretion, issue a summons or an e-summons for the attendance of the accused, and must record his reasons before issuing a warrant in a case where the law provides for a summons. It is the Haryana rule-level recognition of electronic process, and it sits alongside s.144 of the NI Act, which lets a cheque summons go by speed post or an approved courier.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-Ci.2

terms.gloss: The fee payable for issuing and serving the court's process. Volume III is blunt about it: where process fees or other fees are payable, no process is to be issued until they are paid, and on default of payment within a reasonable time the magistrate may dismiss the complaint. It is the sharpest early risk a cheque complainant carries after cognizance, and it is separate from the ten rupee court fee on the complaint itself. In the Punjab and Haryana courts the process money handed in with stamped postal envelopes is called talbana.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-Ci.2

terms.gloss: A box placed in the verandah of the court house about an hour before the court sits, into which petitions and applications are dropped. It is opened in the magistrate's presence about fifteen minutes after the court opens, again before the lunch recess and a third time fifteen minutes before rising, and every petition in it is initialled by him. Members of the ministerial establishment are forbidden to receive complaints or petitions directly from lawyers or their clerks. It is the Volume III answer to the counter queue, and the rule-level ancestor of the Panchkula filing window.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.4

terms.gloss: The office note or report put up to the magistrate on a petition before he can pass orders on it. Volume III has the magistrate either pass proper orders on a petition forthwith or tell the petitioner when the orders will be ready, once the necessary kaifiyats have been put up. It is one of the Urdu-derived establishment words that the Punjab and Haryana courts still run on, alongside ahlmad, nazir, peshi and talbana.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.4

terms.gloss: The register in which the dates of hearing of the cases before a court are entered. Volume III makes the presiding officer himself fix fresh dates in the peshi register when an unexpected holiday or absence wipes out a day's list, and then hand the register to the reader of the court, who is responsible for telling the parties and witnesses who turn up at a closed court what their new date is. It is the paper ancestor of the CIS cause list, and 'peshi' remains the everyday word for a date of appearance in a Haryana court.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.10

terms.gloss: The direction that once the examination of witnesses has begun the proceedings continue from day to day until the witnesses in attendance have been examined, with reasons recorded in writing for any adjournment beyond the following day. Volume III repeats it twice, for speedy disposal generally and for the stage after the accusation is put. It is the local counterpart of s.143(3) of the NI Act, which asks that a cheque trial be concluded within six months of the filing of the complaint, and the standard against which the years a NACT case actually takes are measured.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-D.11

terms.gloss: The lighter record a summons case and a summary trial get. In a summons case the record is ordinarily a memorandum of the substance of the evidence and no more; in a summary case in which no appeal lies no evidence need be recorded at all, only the prescribed particulars in the summary register, but where an appeal does lie the magistrate must record the substance of the evidence and the particulars, and write a judgment before passing sentence. Since a cheque case is tried summarily and carries an appeal, this is the shape of the trial record a s.138 file actually ends up with. It is also what the judgment writer has to reconstruct from the file: what the complainant tendered, under which exhibit number, and the date on which the evidence was closed - Volume III r.1-H.1(i-b) requires exhibits to be referred to by their number and not only by name, and BNSS s.286 lists the particulars a summary record must carry.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-E.8
aka: memorandum of the substance of the evidence

terms.gloss: Dismissal of a complaint case because the complainant did not appear. Volume III opens the chapter with the warning that some magistrates are inclined to dismiss cases in default hastily, and then requires the magistrate to consider whether such an order is legal and whether it is justified by the circumstances, and to record his reasons in every case. A complainant absent when the case is first called must have it called again later, and the time of dismissal must be noted on the record. This is the check a dismissed cheque complaint is revived on, in revision.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-F.2
aka: dismissal for absence of the complainant

terms.gloss: In a summons case instituted on a complaint, if the complainant fails to attend on a day fixed for hearing the accused is to be acquitted, unless the magistrate adjourns the hearing or dispenses with the complainant's attendance and proceeds. A s.138 case is tried as a summons case, so this is not a mere dismissal - the accused walks free on the merits, and the complainant's remedy is revision, not a fresh complaint. It is the procedural risk the complainant carries on every single date.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-D.5
aka: acquittal for non-appearance of the complainant

terms.gloss: The Volume III rule that a fine, though the lightest punishment a criminal court can impose, must never be excessive with reference to the means of the offender. Indiscriminate fines only waste the time of the courts and the police in trying to realise them and harass the convict and his dependants. On a s.138 conviction the fine may run to twice the amount of the cheque, so this is the state-level counterweight a Haryana magistrate applies when fixing it, and the reason the sentence in default is set with the status of the accused in mind.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 19-B.1
aka: fine in proportion to the offender's means
capacity of the convict to pay

terms.gloss: Imprisonment ordered to be served if the fine is not paid. Volume III confirms that criminal courts are empowered to impose it but only subject to the limits the penal code sets, and asks that it be regulated with regard to the status of the accused so that he is induced to pay rather than to evade payment. In a cheque case, where the fine can be twice the cheque amount, the default sentence is often the only thing that actually moves money.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 19-B.2
aka: imprisonment in default of payment of fine

terms.gloss: Where an offender is sentenced to a fine and to imprisonment in default and does not pay at once, the court may order that the fine be paid within a stated period or by instalments. Volume III points the magistrate at the power expressly. In a s.138 case this is the ordinary route by which a convicted drawer pays the cheque amount over to the complainant without going to jail, and it is the sentencing side of the settlements that end most cheque cases.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 19-B.3
aka: postponement of realisation of the fine

terms.gloss: The court's treasurer and custodian. The nazir holds cash and property in the court's keeping, and pays out the money side of a case: the memorandum of the costs of witnesses is made out and forwarded to him, and property sent in by the police is made over to him for custody. The office is the nazarat branch. In a cheque case the nazir is who a witness's diet and road money comes from, and where a fine or a deposit is lodged.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 9-A.3

terms.gloss: The daily allowance, with road money, paid to a witness who attends a criminal court. Volume III sets out when the court pays these expenses and carries a whole set of State instructions written for the nazarat officers and the presiding officers to prevent fraud and embezzlement in their disbursement. In a cheque case they are what the bank official who proves the return memo is entitled to, and one of the practical reasons a bank witness is better examined over a live link.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 9-B.1

terms.gloss: The officer who administers e-filing. Under the E-Filing Rules the Administrator is, for the High Court, the Registrar (IT) or an officer appointed by the Chief Justice, and for a district court the officer or official appointed by the District and Sessions Judge. Everything that has to be unlocked in an e-filed case goes through him, including transferring an action from a litigant in person to the advocate later engaged. This is the formal name for the office the Panchkula filing assistants call the computer room and telephone before an e-filed NACT case can be released into their queue.
terms.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 3.2

terms.gloss: The defined term that decides whether the e-filing regime reaches a cheque case at all. An Action under the E-Filing Rules includes all proceedings instituted in the court or tribunal, and criminal complaints are named expressly, alongside suits, petitions, appeals, revisions and interlocutory applications. So a s.138 complaint is inside the e-filing rules and not merely a civil-side facility, and every rule that follows - formatting, digital signature, court fees, retention of originals, computation of time - applies to it.
terms.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 3.1

terms.gloss: A counter at which a case can be filed electronically over the court's intranet instead of over the internet, together with the e-Service Centres provided for the purpose. The E-Filing Rules apply to both online e-filing and e-filing through designated counters, and filing at a counter is permitted up to 1600 hours on a court working day. For a filer who has no digital signature, or whose document will not scan, this is the staffed alternative to the portal - and the point at which the e-filing regime meets the physical filing window.
terms.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2

terms.gloss: The date on which an action is treated as filed electronically: the date it is received in the Registry within the prescribed time on a working day, reckoned in Indian Standard Time. Online filing after midnight counts as the next day, and filing on a gazetted holiday or a day the court is closed counts as the next working day; failure of the portal is no ground for exemption from limitation. Limitation is otherwise the same regime as physical filing. This is what fixes whether a cheque complaint is inside the one month allowed by s.142(1)(b) of the NI Act.
terms.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 15

terms.gloss: The duty on a party who e-files scanned documents to keep the originals for production or inspection as the court directs, to preserve a signed vakalatnama or an attested affidavit for at least two years after final disposal including appeal, and to bear the burden of producing the originals and proving they are genuine. Some documents must be kept permanently - and a negotiable instrument is one of them, except a cheque. So the cheque, which is the whole of a s.138 case, sits under the ordinary rule and has to be produced when the court calls for it.
terms.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 11

terms.gloss: The form an e-filed document has to take. All original typed material must be prepared as the Rules and Orders require and converted into an optical-character-recognition searchable PDF, and documents that are not text - scans, photographs - must be scanned to the stated standard. It is the bar the cheque, the bank return memo and the demand notice have to clear before an e-filed cheque complaint will be accepted, and the reason the Panchkula assistants ask for a clean PDF copy of a physical file.
terms.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 7

terms.gloss: A live television link or other audio-video electronic arrangement by which a person who is physically absent from the courtroom is nevertheless virtually present in it, to give evidence and be cross-examined. The Video Conferencing Rules make video conferencing available at all stages of a judicial proceeding and treat a proceeding conducted that way as a judicial proceeding for every purpose, using the software the High Court designates. Chapter 1 Part BB of Volume III is what carries these Rules into the criminal courts where a cheque case is tried.
terms.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(ix)

terms.gloss: The courtroom, or any place where the court is physically convened, in a hearing held over a live link - including the place where a commissioner or an inquiring officer holds proceedings on the court's directions. It is the anchor end of a video-conferenced hearing: the judge, the record and the coordinator who runs the link sit at the Court Point, and a document at the Court Point is shown to a remote witness by transmitting an image of it.
terms.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(v)

terms.gloss: The place where a person appears or is examined through a video link. It may be another court, a legal services authority or mediation centre, a jail, a hospital, or an Indian consulate abroad, and the Rules name who acts as coordinator at each. A summons to a witness who is to be examined by video conferencing must state the date, time and venue of the Remote Point and direct him to attend there in person with proof of identity. In a cheque case this is usually where the out-of-station complainant or the bank official appears from.
terms.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(x)

terms.gloss: The defined class of people who may take part in a hearing over a live link: the person to be examined, the person in whose presence proceedings are to be recorded, an advocate or a party in person who intends to examine a witness, anyone required to make submissions, and anyone else the court permits to appear by video conferencing. In a s.138 case it covers the complainant, the accused whose personal attendance has been dispensed with, and the bank witness.
terms.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(xii)

terms.gloss: The official who runs a video-conferenced hearing at each end. There is a coordinator at the Court Point and, where a witness or an accused is to be examined, one at the Remote Point as well; in the district judiciary they are nominated by the High Court or the District Judge. Who it is depends on where the remote end sits - a consular official abroad, a nominated official of another district court, the jail superintendent, a medical superintendent, or an officer of the legal services authority. The coordinator identifies the person appearing, and identifies and accounts for anyone else present at the Remote Point.
terms.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 5

terms.gloss: A piece of software a High Court or district court builds for itself alongside CIS, because the CIS core cannot be changed locally. A peripheral application reads case data through an API - case type, case status, case number, party name - and cannot write anything back into CIS. Punjab and Haryana runs three of them, written in-house in PHP: the Surety module, Crystal CIS Reports and a s.138 tool. The read-only limit is the boundary any court-facing system has to design around: it can show and cross-check what CIS holds, but the case record itself is only ever written inside CIS.
terms.source: e-Courts CIS architecture as described by the IT wing of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The in-house application in which a person offering surety for an accused is recorded, with an Aadhaar number, and checked against every other court in Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh to see whether he is a repeat or habitual surety. A person who has already stood surety may stand again, but must produce a different document each time - a motorcycle registration certificate, then a car registration certificate, then a mortgage of property. It puts into software the declaration BNSS §486 already requires of every surety and the stock-surety concern behind Rules and Orders Volume III r.10.9. The database sits centrally at the High Court; it cannot see any other state, so a surety standing repeatedly across state lines is invisible to it.
terms.source: Rules and Orders, Volume III, rule 10.9 (surety and identity documents), read with BNSS §486; the module itself described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: A person who stands surety again and again, for strangers and for a consideration, rather than out of any real connection with the accused. Rules and Orders Volume III r.10.9(9A) was added in 2007 to stop accused persons absconding on a bogus surety or a bond furnished by a stock surety: in the classes of case it covers, the surety must give two passport photographs no more than six months old, one kept in the court record and one with the police station, together with a passport, election identity card, PAN card, bank card, government identity card or any other document ordinarily issued after verification of identity and address. BNSS §486 goes wider and makes every surety declare how many people he has already stood surety for.
terms.source: Rules and Orders, Volume III, rule 10.9(9A) (added 2007), read with BNSS §486 and §140

terms.gloss: CCR, the reporting application the High Court's technical wing built in-house because some of the reports CIS produces are not usable. It runs on each district's own server, since it can only read that district's local CIS data, and the Statement Clerk uses it to produce the monthly returns the High Court's branches ask for - cases registered, cases not registered and the reason, summonses issued, cases listed, cause lists, pendency by stage, and how many cases moved from one court to another on a given date, in a single click.
terms.source: In-house peripheral application of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, described by its IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The official posted in each district court who generates the periodical statements and returns the High Court requires - what was registered, what was not and why, what was listed, what is pending and at which stage. The duty is old: Rules and Orders Volume III r.2.6 makes a magistrate exercising summary powers prepare a statement every month of the summary cases received and the progress in disposing of them, which reaches cheque cases because NI Act §143 makes a s.138 complaint triable summarily, and r.11-A.15 speaks of quarterly statistical returns and of the records the statistical writer needs to make them out. In practice the clerk now produces them through the in-house Crystal CIS Reports tool and sends soft copies up.
terms.source: Rules and Orders, Volume III, rules 2.6 and 11-A.15 (periodical statements and statistical returns); the post described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The technical official posted in a district court establishment. There is a System Officer and a System Assistant per district, and at the district headquarters a System Officer with two or three System Assistants depending on how many courts sit there. They run the CIS server and its performance, the hardware and the annual maintenance contract, while the court officials do the data entry. No rule in the corpus creates the post, and it is not the same as the Administrator whom E-Filing Rules r.3.2 appoints for e-filing matters, although this is very probably the office a filing branch means when it says it has to telephone 'the computer room'.
terms.source: District court technical establishment, Punjab and Haryana; described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026). No rule in the corpus creates the post.

terms.gloss: The National Judicial Data Grid, the national store into which every court's case data flows. Each of the district court servers in Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh talks to it directly over whitelisted addresses. Case data reflects in it in real time when the network is up, so a date the reader assigns appears without anything being sent; orders and judgments are the exception and are pushed each evening by running a command.
terms.source: e-Courts Project, Supreme Court eCommittee - National Judicial Data Grid; the local synchronisation described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The National Informatics Centre, which builds and maintains CIS for the courts. A High Court can suggest a change but cannot make one: the suggestion goes to NIC's Pune unit, which acts only after the Supreme Court eCommittee approves it. A small change may be done in a few days; otherwise it waits for the next version patch, into which suggestions from every High Court in India are gathered. NIC also supplies the migration script that moves a court's data from one CIS version to the next, and NIC scientists are posted at the High Court itself.
terms.source: National Informatics Centre, the technical agency for the e-Courts project; its role described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The e-Committee of the Supreme Court of India, which governs the e-Courts project and is the gate every change to CIS has to pass. A High Court's suggestion reaches NIC, but NIC only builds it once the eCommittee agrees; if it does not, the suggestion waits for the next version, and that has meant years. This is why a court that needs something now builds a peripheral application instead of asking for the core to change.
terms.source: e-Committee of the Supreme Court of India, the governing body of the e-Courts project; its role in the change route described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The third machine at a district court location, alongside the two that run CIS, holding a copy of the court's data so that work can continue if the primary fails. E-Filing Rules r.18 is the rule behind it: e-filings are to be stored on an exclusive server maintained under the control and directions of the Court, and a mirror image of them may be kept at a different geographical location for continuity of operations in a disaster, natural calamity or breakdown.
terms.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 18

terms.gloss: The officer who sits with the presiding judge, keeps the daily proceedings and the dates, and raises the objections on a newly filed case before it is registered. Volume III names him separately from the ahlmad: when a holiday or an absence wipes out a day's list, the presiding officer fixes fresh dates in the peshi register himself and hands the register to the reader of the court, who is responsible for telling the parties and witnesses who turn up at a closed court what their new date is. At Panchkula the reader and the ahlmad are two different desks - the reader owns the daily proceedings and the dates, the ahlmad owns registration, process and the record.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.10; described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The CIS function through which the ahlmad turns a judicial order into an actual piece of process. He opens the court and the date, picks the process type from a numbered list (summons to accused, summons to witness, warrant, and a separate entry for the s.138 summons), generates it, and publishes it. Until it is published the document prints 'Draft' across it and cannot be used. Volume III sends the detailed instructions on issuing and serving process to Volume IV, Chapter 8; what the Sanhita requires of the finished article is that it be signed and sealed, or digitally signed if electronic.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-Ci.6 (mode of issuing and serving process); the CIS process-generation module, described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The summons issued to an accused in a s.138 cheque case, which in CIS is a separate template from the ordinary criminal summons and prints in a different, larger format. It has its own service regime: s.144 of the NI Act lets the magistrate direct service by speed post or by a courier approved by a Court of Session, and an acknowledgment or a refusal endorsement lets the court declare service complete. Since the November 2018 amendment to Volume III the magistrate may issue it as an e-summons.
terms.source: NI Act s.144 (mode of service of summons in cheque cases); Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-Ci.2; the distinct CIS template described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The step that turns a generated process from a draft into a live document. Before publishing, the printout carries 'Draft' in large letters and is not acceptable for use; publishing is what commits it. The legal reason is exact: a summons must be in writing signed by the presiding officer and bear the seal of the court, or be in an electronic form bearing the image of the seal or a digital signature, and a warrant must likewise be signed and sealed - a draft carries none of that, so it is not process at all.
terms.source: CIS process-generation workflow, described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026); the requirement it satisfies is in BNSS s.63 and s.72

terms.gloss: What the staff of a Haryana criminal court call the moment the substance of the accusation is put to the accused. In a summons case, and so in a cheque case tried summarily, the particulars of the offence are stated to the accused and he is asked whether he pleads guilty or has any defence, and no formal charge is framed. The everyday phrasing at the desk is that 'charge will be framed' - this and this is alleged against you, you took this much money, what do you say - but in law it is a statement of the particulars, not a charge.
terms.source: BNSS s.274 (substance of accusation to be stated), formerly CrPC s.251; Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-D.2; the local usage recorded firsthand from the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The step a Haryana magistrate's court takes when bailable and non-bailable warrants keep coming back unserved: it writes to the drawer's bank for the KYC address on the account, on the footing that the address the complainant supplied may be false or stale, and then re-issues process to the address the bank returns. No rule prescribes it. It rests on the court's ordinary power to summon a document or thing, and on the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, under which a court may order a party to be at liberty to inspect and take copies of entries in a banker's book.
terms.source: A local coercive-execution step described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026); the powers it rests on are BNSS s.94 and the Bankers' Books Evidence Act s.6

terms.gloss: Sending a finished case file down to the court's record room for keeping. When judgment is pronounced the file comes back to the ahlmad, who binds it, generates the index proforma and consigns it. Volume III's standing requirement is that the record be complete before it is consigned, and that a proceeding which is separate from the main case - a transfer application, and by the same logic a criminal miscellaneous matter - be consigned to the record room separately from it.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 3.18 and rule 26-B.1; the binding-and-sending practice described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The proforma the ahlmad generates out of CIS for a decided case and attaches to the bound file before consigning it to the record room; it lists what the record contains. CIS can produce the same index for a pending file. It is the modern form of Volume III's requirement that the record be complete before it goes to the record room - the retention and indexing rules themselves sit in Rules and Orders Volumes IV and VI-B, which are not yet in this corpus.
terms.source: CIS report, described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026); the completeness requirement it serves is in Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 3.18

terms.gloss: A miscellaneous criminal proceeding taken out of a case that has already been decided and consigned - an application on a NACT file that has gone to the record room, for instance. It is separated from the parent file and becomes a fresh file with its own number, obtained from the filing branch downstairs. Volume III states the same principle for transfer applications: they must form a file separate from the record of the main case and be consigned to the record room separately.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 26-B.1; the CRM separation described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The register of cases instituted in the court. Volume III requires a summary case to be entered in Register No. 1 as soon as it is received in court, and again in the register of summary cases when the accused appears, and makes the ahlmad the keeper of the court's registers subject to a monthly inspection by the presiding officer. In Panchkula the register is now fed from the database: the ahlmad runs the month's institution report out of e-Courts for the establishment and case type, prints it, and pastes it into the physical register.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 2.6 and rule 11-A.14; the e-Courts print-and-paste method described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The case-management reporting the High Court requires of each court, which at Panchkula means a running list of two hundred cases kept updated almost daily out of a pendency of about a thousand, alongside some twenty to thirty other statements. Its rule-level ancestors are in Volume III: every judicial officer must send the High Court a monthly statement of criminal cases pending over one year in the prescribed proforma before the 10th of the following month, with history sheets for the six oldest, and daily progress reports besides. The ahlmad assembles it himself in a spreadsheet, because the reports CIS gives are not aligned with what the High Court asks for.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.12, rule 1-A.13 and rule 1-A.11; the current High Court format described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The summary statement of a court's work - the balance sheet of institution, disposal and pendency - that the staff prepare from the CIS management report for the monthly return to the High Court. The word is the everyday Punjab and Haryana term for such an abstract. Volume III's periodical statements are what it feeds: the monthly statement of criminal cases pending over one year, and the monthly statement of summary cases received and disposed of.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.12 and rule 2.6; the word and the CIS balance-sheet source recorded firsthand from the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The court official who prepares the written judgment. At Panchkula he is a stenographer-cadre post working inside the courtroom and chambers, distinct from the stenographer outside who takes the daily orders: the steno outside does daily orders, the judgment writer does judgments. He reads the decided file end to end, lifts the case metadata and the template out of CIS, copies the cause title, the parties, the appearances and the facts off the paper file, records the proceedings and the evidence, takes the judge's dictation of the arguments and conclusion in shorthand, types the transcript, and then uploads and e-signs it. Volume III r.25-G.8 recognises the function - stenographers typing evidence and judgments from dictation, and duplicating the free copies in advance - and BNSS s.288(2) allows a summary-trial record or judgment to be prepared by an officer appointed for the purpose, the magistrate signing it. The title itself, and the split between daily-order and judgment stenographers, are establishment practice and appear in no rule.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 25-G.8; the post and the split of duties described firsthand by a judgment writer at the Panchkula district courts (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The order recorded for a case on each date of hearing - the running order sheet of the file. It is where the court records who appeared and who represented whom, which is why the judgment writer reads the previous daily orders back to build the appearance block of the judgment, cross-checking them against the power of attorney pinned at the back of the file. The daily orders are the stenographer-outside's work; the judgment is the judgment writer's. Nothing about appearance reaches the case record in a queryable form, so it has to be read off the sheet. Staff at Panchkula were heard to call these the 'zimni' orders, the Punjab and Haryana word for the running order sheet.
terms.source: Court practice, Punjab and Haryana district courts; described firsthand by a judgment writer at the Panchkula district courts (PUCAR interview, June 2026). The word 'zimni' is from the machine transcript of the Hindi audio and is recorded as heard; the uploader's own English subtitles render the same thing as 'daily orders'.

terms.gloss: The physical register in which a convicting court records its convictions and takes the convict's acknowledgment for the free copy of the judgment. The convict signs 'copy received' in the corner, and against it the entry has to carry the case and registration number, the accused's name, the sentence and the compensation or fine. It is kept on paper and is not held in CIS. Volume III does not itself prescribe it - the numbered criminal registers sit in Rules and Orders Volumes IV and VI-B, which are not yet in this corpus, and Volume III's own conviction-reporting duty in Chapter 11 Part G covers a listed set of Penal Code and special-Act offences that does not include the Negotiable Instruments Act. At Panchkula it is no longer handwritten: the details are copied out of the judgment into MS Word, shortened, printed, cut and pasted in, a whole month at a time.
terms.source: Court register kept by the judgment writer, Panchkula district courts, described firsthand (PUCAR interview, June 2026). The register series itself is prescribed in Rules and Orders Volumes IV and VI-B, which are not in this corpus; Volume III rule 2.3 and rule 26-B.2 show how it refers registers out.

terms.gloss: The copy of the judgment a convicted accused gets without paying for it, so that he can appeal. Volume III r.1-H.1(vi) requires that whenever an accused is sentenced to imprisonment a copy of the finding and sentence be given to him free of cost soon after the delivery of the judgment, and BNSS s.404(1) says the same of the judgment itself, immediately after pronouncement; s.404(2) makes a certified copy free of cost in every case where the judgment is appealable by the accused, on his application. It matters because BNSS s.423 requires a petition of appeal to be accompanied by a copy of the judgment appealed against. At Panchkula it is treated as a right that needs no request and is handed over the same day, the convict signing for it in the conviction register - which is wider than the letter of s.404(2), and is the shape Volume III r.25-G.2 to r.25-G.4 give the free supply for appeal and revision.
terms.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-H.1(vi) and rules 25-G.2 to 25-G.4, read with BNSS s.404 (formerly CrPC s.363); the same-day handover practice described firsthand by a judgment writer at the Panchkula district courts (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

terms.gloss: The monthly assurance a court official signs and sends to the main office of the establishment, stating that for the preceding month all the orders and judgments have been uploaded. It is a single printed format carrying no case numbers and no counts, only the blanket statement, and at Panchkula it goes down around the third of the month. No rule in the corpus creates it; it belongs to the e-Courts era and sits alongside the older periodical statements Volume III requires - the monthly statement of criminal cases pending over a year, and the monthly statement of summary cases received and disposed of. CIS already reports which orders are still pending upload, which is the report the writer runs for himself before signing.
terms.source: District court reporting practice, Panchkula, described firsthand by a judgment writer (PUCAR interview, June 2026). No provision in this corpus prescribes it; its rule-level ancestors are Rules and Orders Volume III rules 1-A.12 and 2.6.

terms.gloss: The magistrate on the duty roster, before whom work is put up that cannot wait for the court it belongs to. The month is divided among the judges of the establishment in blocks of a few days each, and whatever arises for a court that is on leave goes to whoever holds duty - police remands, bail applications and miscellaneous applications. It is a court-administration arrangement created by no rule in this corpus, but the work it brings is governed: Volume III requires the reasons for a remand to police custody to be recorded and a copy sent to the District Magistrate, and BNSS s.187 is the live custody provision. None of it is cheque-case work; it reaches the s.138 court's staff through the roster, not the case type.
terms.source: District court duty roster, Panchkula, described firsthand by a judgment writer (PUCAR interview, June 2026). No rule in this corpus creates the roster; the remand duty it carries is in Rules and Orders Volume III rule 11-B.9, read with BNSS s.187.

terms.gloss: Signing a judgment or order inside CIS with a digital signature held on a pen-drive token, so that it can be uploaded as a signed document. Orders can be signed and uploaded in a batch, but each one still has to be selected individually, and there is no bulk download. The obligation behind it is old: Volume III r.1-H.1(ii) and (iii) and BNSS s.392(3) require the judgment to be dated and signed by the presiding officer, and every page of it where it was not written in his own hand; IT Act s.5 and s.6 give an electronic signature the same legal effect and authorise its use by courts and government. This is not the same as the digital signature or Aadhaar-based e-Sign the E-Filing Rules require of a party or advocate on an e-filed document.
terms.source: CIS judgment and order workflow, described firsthand by a judgment writer at the Panchkula district courts (PUCAR interview, June 2026); the signature requirement it satisfies is in Rules and Orders Volume III rule 1-H.1 and BNSS s.392, and its legal effect in IT Act sections 5 and 6

story.summary: How a s.138 (cheque bounce, 'NACT') case runs in Haryana, end to end. It starts at the Panchkula lower-court filing window - submission, scrutiny, CIS entry and same-day dispatch to the trial court, from a June 2026 field interview with the filing assistants - and then follows the case through cognizance, the issue of summons or e-summons, appearance, the summary trial, the evidence, compounding, judgment and sentence, and appeal, grounded in Volume III of the Punjab and Haryana High Court's Rules and Orders and the High Court's E-Filing and Video Conferencing Rules.

process.summary: The whole spine of a NACT case in Haryana. Stages 1 to 4 are the Panchkula lower-court filing window as the filing assistants describe it: receive, scrutinise, enter in CIS, register and dispatch the same day. Stages 5 to 13 are the case after it reaches the trial court, grounded in Volume III of the Punjab and Haryana High Court's Rules and Orders, the Instructions to Criminal Courts, with the E-Filing and Video Conferencing Rules layered on. The last stage collects the self-started workarounds that sit outside any rule.

stages.stage: 1 · Advocate submits the physical file

steps.t: The advocate submits the NACT file at the lower-court filing window (open until 12:00 PM); the filing assistant receives it.
